title: Does Mark Zuckerberg really believe AI is ‘for everyone’?
slides: Does Zuckerberg truly want AI for all?
Meta's Llama is free, but not open.
Its license silently restricts the biggest players.
Your AI projects may already violate the terms.
Check Llama's acceptable use policy before shipping.
thread_text:
1. Who really gets AI?

Meta gives away Llama, but its license quietly bars the biggest tech firms. Your project might be next in line for restrictions.

2. Free isn't open

Llama's 'open' label hides clauses that forbid using it for certain services. Developers often miss this until after launch.

3. The silent cap

If you have over 700 million monthly users, you can't use Llama without explicit Meta approval. A hidden limit that catches giants off guard.

4. Your risk now

Most startups ignore the acceptable use policy, assuming it's boilerplate. A single integration could violate terms and trigger legal actions.

5. Check before shipping

Open Llama's acceptable use policy today. If you don't know what's there, you're already in danger.

instagram.caption:
You’re building on Meta's Llama right now, and its license quietly blocks any service with over 700 million monthly users.  

That "free" model isn't open—it's restricted. The acceptable use policy also bars specific use cases, and most developers never read it until after launch. A single integration can violate those terms and expose you to legal action.  

For you, that means your startup's AI feature might already be in breach. One hidden clause can sink a product you've shipped.  

Go open Llama's policy page before your next deploy. Do you know which line in it applies to your user count? ⚖️📄🚫
